"Nicker" has several distinct meanings depending on the context — a horse-related sense, a British slang sense, a woodworking tool sense, and a less common dialect sense.

This is the most widely known meaning. A nicker is the soft, gentle, low-pitched sound that a horse makes — often described as a rumbling or vibrating sound coming from deep in the throat, with the mouth closed or barely open.

How to picture it: Imagine a horse in a stable. You walk toward it carrying its food. The horse sees you coming and makes a soft, quiet, almost purring rumble. That's a nicker. It is not loud or sharp. It is warm and gentle.

How it differs from similar sounds:

  • A neigh is the loud, long, high-pitched call — the classic horse sound most people know. You can hear it from far away.
  • A whinny is similar to a neigh but shorter and often higher in pitch.
  • A nicker is much quieter and softer than both. It stays low and close. It is an intimate sound.

When do horses nicker?

  • When greeting their owner or a person they know and like
  • When they smell food coming
  • When a mare (mother horse) calls softly to her foal (baby)
  • When one horse greets another nearby horse

So a nicker is essentially a horse's way of saying "Hey, I know you" or "Oh good, you're here" — a sound of contentment, recognition, or gentle anticipation.

Example sentence: The old mare gave a soft nicker when she heard her owner's footsteps approaching the barn.

In British English, a nicker means one pound sterling (£1).

It is informal slang, the kind used in casual everyday speech — not in formal writing or official contexts.

Important detail: Unlike some slang money words, "nicker" does not change to "nickers" when you talk about multiple pounds. The plural stays the same: nicker.

  • ✅ "That'll cost you five nicker." (= £5)
  • ❌ "That'll cost you five nickers." (incorrect)

Example sentences:

  • "It only cost me a nicker." (= It only cost me £1.)
  • "Can you lend me twenty nicker?" (= Can you lend me £20?)

This usage is particularly common in London and other parts of England, and you will often encounter it in British films, TV shows, and everyday conversation.

In the world of woodworking and hand tools, a nicker (sometimes also called a nicker blade or scoring spur) is a small, sharp blade or cutter built into certain woodworking planes and saws.

Its job: When a plane or saw cuts across or against the grain of wood, the wood fibers on the edges can tear, splinter, or become rough and ragged. The nicker prevents this. It is positioned just ahead of the main cutting blade, and it slices cleanly through the wood fibers before the main blade reaches them. This pre-scoring action means the wood gets cut cleanly, with neat, crisp edges rather than torn, rough ones.

Where you find nickers:

  • On combination planes (multi-purpose hand planes used for making grooves, rebates, and decorative moldings in wood)
  • On certain saws, where a small nicker tooth scores the surface before the main teeth cut through

Think of it this way: Imagine trying to tear a piece of thick cardboard with your hands. If you first score a clean line along it with a knife, the tear follows that line perfectly. The nicker does exactly that job — it scores first so the main blade can follow cleanly.

Example sentence: Before cutting the groove, he checked that the nicker on the combination plane was sharp enough to cleanly score the surface.

In certain older British regional dialects, nicker was used to refer to a marble — as in the small, round glass balls that children play with in the game of marbles.

This meaning is rarely encountered today. It belongs mostly to historical or very regional usage, and you are unlikely to come across it in modern everyday language. However, a complete understanding of the word includes knowing it exists.
